proof:
# Strict containment and midpoint-center gains from depth root concavity

For a positive-volume convex body K in R^d, d>=1, define

    A(K)=max_(y in K) min_(u in S^(d-1))
             vol_d(K intersect {x:u.(x-y)>=0}).

This is unnormalized maximum halfspace depth. The through-point formulation
is equivalent to allowing every closed halfspace containing y, since its
boundary can be shifted to y, decreasing its intersection.

The maximum is attained. For K contained in a ball of radius R, changing y
by delta changes each directional cap by at most the volume of a slab of
thickness |delta|, bounded by kappa_(d-1) R^(d-1)|delta|. Taking the infimum
preserves this common Lipschitz bound. Thus the depth function is continuous
on compact K. In dimension1 take kappa_0=1. Positivity follows from an
interior ball. An affine map T transforms A(K) by |det T|.

## Existing root-concavity input

For positive d-dimensional convex bodies K,L and s,t>=0 with s+t>0, accepted fact 4e868f774de77608, applied to the Cayley body of K and L and deepest points in its endpoint fibers, gives

    A(sK+tL)^(1/d) >= s A(K)^(1/d)+t A(L)^(1/d).     (1)

For s,t>0, put lambda=t/(s+t), apply the cited concavity statement at the endpoint deepest points in conv(({0} x K) union ({1} x L)), and then use A((s+t)B)=(s+t)^d A(B). When one coefficient is zero the same formula follows directly from scaling. The case s=t=0 is outside the positive-volume definition of A and is not needed here. This inequality is reused background; the new content below is its strict-containment and actual mixed three-fiber consequences.

## Strict monotonicity under strict convex containment

If K is contained in int(L), compactness supplies epsilon>0 with
K+epsilon B contained in L. Monotonicity at any fixed candidate point gives
A(L)>=A(K+epsilon B). Equation (1) and A(B)=vol(B)/2 imply

    A(L)^(1/d)>=A(K)^(1/d)+epsilon (vol(B)/2)^(1/d)>A(K)^(1/d).

Thus strict containment strictly increases unnormalized maximum depth. No
claim of strict monotonicity for arbitrary non-strict containment is made.

## Three-fiber consequence independent of simplex shape

Let K0,K1,K2 be positive convex bodies with (K0+K2)/2 contained in int(K1).
Their endpoint integer fibers at0 and2 can be isolated, so their restricted
unnormalized depths are A(K0),A(K2). If both endpoints were globally deepest,
these values would equal D. But (1) and strict monotonicity give

    A(K1)>A((K0+K2)/2)>=D.

The middle's own-fiber guarantee is already greater than D, a contradiction.
Therefore at most one endpoint can be globally deepest, without requiring
that any fiber be a simplex or have equal volume to another.


## A stronger mixed three-fiber consequence, including active containment

Let (K0+K2)/2 be contained in K1, with no strictness assumption. Write
D_e=A(Ke)>0 and choose continuous deepest centers y0,y2 in the endpoint
fibers. The actual mixed-integer point y=(1,(y0+y2)/2) has unnormalized mixed
halfspace depth at least

    ((D0^(1/d)+D2^(1/d))/2)^d + min(D0,D2).

For any ambient closed halfspace through y, the middle section contains the
Minkowski average of the endpoint THROUGH-CENTER continuous caps with the
same continuous normal. Their volumes are at least D0,D2, giving the first
term by Brunn--Minkowski. Separately, the ambient halfspace contains at least
one endpoint point (0,y0) or (2,y2), since y is their midpoint. That endpoint
contributes at least its D_e, giving the second term. If the ambient normal
is vertical, the entire middle fiber is present and the same first bound
follows from ordinary volume Brunn--Minkowski; an endpoint is still present.

In particular D0=D2=D forces middle mixed depth at least2D. Thus both endpoint
fibers cannot be globally deepest in any such positive three-fiber family.
